## Overview

The lecture opens by completing the discrete picture with DDIM [@ddim], which keeps DDPM's marginals $q(x_t\mid x_0)$ while dropping the Markov property of the forward process, so one trained network can be sampled in many ways --- from a deterministic sampler ($\eta=0$) to DDPM itself ($\eta=1$). That construction is built in @sec-ddim, next to DDPM, and @sec-recall recalls the three facts from it that this chapter uses.

This chapter is what comes after: the lecture moves to continuous time, following @sde. Score matching with Langevin dynamics (SMLD) of @song2019ncsn and DDPM turn out to be discretizations of two stochastic differential equations, and running such an SDE backwards only requires the score $\nabla_{x}\log p_t$ at every noise level. So training a diffusion model is the same as training a score function, and for the VP SDE the denoising score matching loss coincides with the DDPM loss.

The lecture closes with a geometric explanation of why diffusion models work better than GANs --- diffusion as a scale-space of the data distribution, with the samples at each noise level on a thin shell around the data manifold. Lecture 08 opened by going through the same argument, so the two accounts are merged in the chapter [Why Diffusion Models](why-diffusion.qmd), which follows this one.

Most of the claims below are checked numerically in @sec-worked, on a one-dimensional example where every score is known exactly.

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $x_0\sim p_0 = p_{\text{data}}$, $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ | clean data |
| $\alpha_t = 1-\beta_t$, $\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s\le t}\alpha_s$, $\bar\alpha_0=1$ | DDPM noise schedule |
| $\gamma_t$, $\eta$, $\tilde\beta_t$ | standard deviation of the reverse step of the $\eta$ family, $\gamma_t=\eta\sqrt{\tilde\beta_t}$, with $\tilde\beta_t$ the posterior *variance* of @sec-ddim |
| $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$, $\hat{x}_t$ | noise predictor and Tweedie estimate of $x_0$ |
| $p_t$, $p_{0t}(x_t\mid x_0)$ | marginal of $x(t)$ and transition kernel (written $p_{0i}$ on the slides) |
| $s_\theta(x,t)$ | score network (written $s_\theta(x,i)$ on the slides) |
| $f$, $g$, $w$, $\bar{w}$ | drift, diffusion coefficient, forward and reverse Wiener processes |
| $\sigma_t$, $\beta(t)$ | VE noise level and VP noise rate |
| $\Delta = \nabla\cdot\nabla$ | Laplacian |

: Notation for the continuous-time formulation. Symbols shared with
  the discrete chapters keep their meaning there. {#tbl-notation-sde}

Throughout this chapter $t$ increases with the noise level, whereas slides 43, 46 index time in the opposite direction. We write fresh Gaussian noise as $z$ (slides 23, 24 write $\epsilon$), so that $\epsilon$ always means the noise that produced $x_t$. The DDIM standard deviation is $\gamma_t$, written $\sigma_t$ on slides 17, 23. Slide 24 writes $\epsilon^{(t)}_{\theta^*}$ and $x^{(t)}_{\theta^*}$ for what we call $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ and $\hat{x}_t$, and slide 32 indexes the SMLD sampler by $i$, as we do in @eq-ve-sampler. Fresh noise is $z$ and $\epsilon$ is the noise that produced $x_t$, the same split the discrete chapters use.

## What chapter 6 already gives us {#sec-recall}

The lecture opens with the DDIM construction of slides 17--25. This book does
not keep that boundary: DDIM is defined entirely in DDPM's terms --- the same
noisy marginals, the same network, the same loss --- so it is built next to
DDPM in @sec-ddim rather than restated here. Three results from there are used
throughout this chapter, and it is worth having them in view.

**The $\eta$ family.** For any $\gamma$ with $0\le\gamma_t^2\le1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}$
there is a forward process, non-Markov in general, with DDPM's marginals
$q(x_t\mid x_0)$ and the same noise-regression loss, so one trained network
serves every member. Writing $\gamma_t=\eta\sqrt{\tilde\beta_t}$ indexes the
family by a single $\eta$, with $\eta=1$ the DDPM ancestral sampler and
$\eta=0$ a deterministic map from $x_T$ to $x_0$ (@sec-ddim-exact). Skipping
steps along a subsequence $\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_S$ is @sec-skip.

**The reverse step in three parts.** Every member of the family writes one
reverse step as Tweedie's denoiser, parametric noise and stochastic noise,
@eq-denoise-renoise. Slide 54 restates this decomposition once the SDE is in
place, which the next chapter does where it builds the noisy manifolds.

**Noise prediction and the score are the same object.**
$s_\theta=-\epsilon_\theta/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$, with Tweedie's formula as
its companion identity (@eq-epsilon-score-conversion). This is what lets the
discrete chapters and the continuous one below be read as one theory, and the
VP SDE below uses it to show that the DDPM loss *is* denoising score matching.

What belongs to this chapter is everything that only makes sense once the SDE
exists: that SMLD, DDPM and DDIM are three discretizations of one equation
(slide 36), that the deterministic sampler is a discretization of the
probability flow ODE, and the geometric argument of slides 39--54 for why any
of it works.

## The SDE formulation

### Forward and reverse SDEs

We now let the number of steps go to infinity. Starting from $x(0)\sim p_0$, the data evolve according to the Ito SDE

$$
dx = f(x,t)\,dt + g(t)\,dw,\qquad
\text{which means}\qquad x(t+\Delta t)\approx x(t)+f\,\Delta t + g\sqrt{\Delta t}\,z
$$ {#eq-forward-sde}

for small $\Delta t$, where $f$ and $g$ are chosen so that $x(T)\sim p_T$ is a simple Gaussian. The second form is the Euler-Maruyama step.

To reverse the process we need to know how the density $p_t$ evolves in time. This evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation (the general version is on slide 51 and in the next chapter),

$$
\partial_t p_t = -\nabla\cdot(f\,p_t) + \tfrac12 g^2\Delta p_t = -\nabla\cdot\Big(\big[f-\tfrac12 g^2\nabla\log p_t\big]p_t\Big),
$$ {#eq-fp}

where the second form uses $\nabla p_t = p_t\nabla\log p_t$. To derive the equation, take a smooth test function $\varphi$. Ito's formula gives $\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}\varphi(x) = \mathbb{E}[\nabla\varphi\cdot f + \frac12g^2\Delta\varphi]$, because the noise term has mean zero. The left side is $\int\varphi\,\partial_tp_t\,dx$. On the right, integrating by parts moves the derivatives from $\varphi$ onto $p_t$ and gives $\int\varphi\,[-\nabla\cdot(fp_t)+\frac12g^2\Delta p_t]\,dx$. Since the two agree for every $\varphi$, @eq-fp follows [@sarkka2019].

::: {#thm-reverse}
## Reverse-time SDE
If we run
$$
dx = \big[f(x,t) - g(t)^2\nabla_{x}\log p_t(x)\big]dt + g(t)\,d\bar{w}
$$ {#eq-reverse-sde}
backwards in time from $x(T)\sim p_T$ (so that $dt<0$), then the solution has marginal $p_t$ at every time $t$ [@anderson1982]. In particular, $x(0)\sim p_0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We only show that the marginals agree, which is all that sampling requires. Anderson's theorem also identifies the law of whole paths. Let $q_\tau = p_{T-\tau}$. From @eq-fp we get
$\partial_\tau q_\tau = \nabla\cdot([f-\frac12g^2\nabla\log q_\tau]q_\tau) = -\nabla\cdot([-f+g^2\nabla\log q_\tau]q_\tau) + \frac12g^2\Delta q_\tau$,
where we added and subtracted $\frac12g^2\Delta q_\tau = \nabla\cdot(\frac12g^2q_\tau\nabla\log q_\tau)$. This is the Fokker-Planck equation of $dx = [-f+g^2\nabla\log p_{T-\tau}]d\tau + g\,dw_\tau$, and substituting $t = T-\tau$ gives @eq-reverse-sde.
:::

The reverse drift is thus the forward drift minus $g^2$ times the score, and the score is the only unknown quantity. The reversal holds in distribution, not for individual paths. If we follow a forward path and then run the reverse SDE from its end point, we do not return to where we started, but the distribution at every time is the same. The figure on slide 29 makes this point, and @fig-sde shows it on our example.

### The probability flow ODE

@eq-fp is a continuity equation with velocity $f-\frac12g^2\nabla\log p_t$, so the deterministic ODE

$$
\frac{dx}{dt} = f(x,t) - \tfrac12 g(t)^2\nabla\log p_t(x)
$$ {#eq-pf-ode}

has the same marginals as the SDE. Its trajectories are the white curves in the figure on slide 29.

For the VP SDE introduced below, this ODE is closely connected to DDIM. Change variables to $\bar{x} = x/\sqrt{\bar\alpha}$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{(1-\bar\alpha)/\bar\alpha}$. Then $\bar{x} = x_0+\sigma\epsilon$, so $\sigma$ is the VE noise level of the rescaled variable. Using $\dot{\bar\alpha} = -\beta\bar\alpha$ and @eq-epsilon-score-conversion, we find

$$
\frac{d\bar{x}}{dt} = -\frac{\beta\,\nabla\log p_t}{2\sqrt{\bar\alpha}} = \frac{\beta\,\epsilon^*}{2\sqrt{\bar\alpha(1-\bar\alpha)}},\qquad
\frac{d\sigma}{dt} = \frac{\beta}{2\sqrt{\bar\alpha(1-\bar\alpha)}},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad \frac{d\bar{x}}{d\sigma} = \epsilon^*.
$$ {#eq-pf-sigma}

Taking one Euler step of this ODE from $\sigma_t$ to $\sigma_{t-1}$ and multiplying by $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}$ gives $x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\hat{x}_t + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\epsilon_\theta$, which is exactly the $\eta=0$ DDIM step. So DDIM is the Euler method for the probability flow ODE written in the variables $(\sigma,\bar{x})$, which is the sense in which slide 36 calls DDIM a special case of the SDE framework.

![The two-mode example under the VP SDE with exact scores, with $p_t$ shown in grey. (a) Forward SDE paths. (b) Reverse SDE paths started from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. They differ from the forward paths but have the same marginals, and they reach the two modes in proportions 0.2 and 0.8. (c) Probability flow ODE paths, which are deterministic and never cross. This is a numerical version of the figure on slide 29.](figures/lec07/HaJunHyun-sde-paths.png){#fig-sde width=100%}

### Which score do we need?

The reverse drift in @eq-reverse-sde at time $t$ requires the score of $p_t$, not the score $\nabla\log p_0$ of the clean data, so the score has to be learned at every noise level and not only at $t=0$.

The clean score is also hard to learn. An empirical distribution has no score at all, and the low-density regions between modes contain very few samples. The clean score carries information about the relative weight of the modes only in these regions, which a sampler rarely visits, and elsewhere it simply pulls towards the nearer mode, as panel (a) of @fig-score shows. Transitions between modes happen at high noise levels, where the modes have merged. The figure of @kim2023dmcmc on slides 30, 43 illustrates this, with an MCMC chain that crosses between modes at a high noise level before the reverse process brings it back down. Langevin dynamics with the clean score does have $p_0$ as its stationary distribution, but crossing the gap takes far longer than any practical run [@song2019ncsn]. In panel (b) of @fig-score, 2000 steps started from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ leave 49 percent of the samples on the mode of weight 0.2 and 51 percent on the mode of weight 0.8, which is where the starting points fell. The reverse SDE recovers the correct proportions.

![(a) The exact score of the two-mode example at $t=0$, $0.25$ and $0.5$. At $t=0$ it is a steep pull towards the nearer mode with an abrupt switch in between, while at larger $t$ it becomes a smooth field that connects the modes. (b) Samples from Langevin dynamics with the clean score (2000 steps of size 0.01 from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$) compared with the reverse SDE.](figures/lec07/HaJunHyun-score-levels.png){#fig-score width=100%}

### Score matching

The objective on slide 31, which we call explicit score matching (ESM), is

$$
J_{\text{ESM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t\,\mathbb{E}_{x_t\sim p_t}\big\Vert s_\theta(x_t,t)-\nabla\log p_t(x_t)\big\Vert_2^2 .
$$ {#eq-esm}

It cannot be computed, because $p_t = \int p_{0t}(\cdot\mid x_0)p_0(x_0)dx_0$ depends on the unknown $p_0$. The lecture instead conditions on $x_0$, for which the kernel $p_{0t}(x_t\mid x_0)$ is known, and this leads to

$$
J_{\text{DSM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t\,\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_0}\,\mathbb{E}_{x_t\sim p_{0t}(\cdot\mid x_0)}\big\Vert s_\theta(x_t,t)-\nabla_{x_t}\log p_{0t}(x_t\mid x_0)\big\Vert_2^2 .
$$ {#eq-dsm}

Slides 31, 33, 35 leave the expectation over $x_0$ implicit.

::: {#thm-dsm}
## Denoising score matching
If differentiation in $x_t$ can be exchanged with integration over $x_0$, then for every $t$ the two objectives differ only by a constant $C_t$ that does not depend on $\theta$ [@vincent2011]. They therefore have the same gradient and the same minimizer, $s_{\theta^*}(\cdot,t) = \nabla\log p_t$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Expand both squares. The term $\mathbb{E}\Vert s_\theta(x_t)\Vert^2$ is the same in both objectives, since $x_t\sim p_t$ in each case. The cross terms also agree, because
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}_{p_t}[s_\theta\cdot\nabla\log p_t] &= \int s_\theta\cdot\nabla p_t\,dx\\
&= \iint s_\theta(x)\cdot\nabla_{x}\log p_{0t}(x\mid x_0)\,p_{0t}(x\mid x_0)\,p_0(x_0)\,dx_0\,dx\\
&= \mathbb{E}_{x_0,x_t}[s_\theta\cdot\nabla\log p_{0t}].
\end{aligned}
$$
The remaining terms do not involve $\theta$. The minimizer of the DSM objective is the conditional mean $\mathbb{E}[\nabla\log p_{0t}(x_t\mid x_0)\mid x_t]$, which by the same exchange equals $\nabla p_t/p_t$.
:::

The constant $C_t$ is the expected conditional variance of the target, so the DSM loss remains positive even at the optimum. In @sec-worked, at $t=0.3$, the difference $J_{\text{DSM}}-J_{\text{ESM}}$ is about 0.570 for three different models.

### SMLD as the VE SDE

SMLD perturbs the data at noise levels $\sigma_1<\dots<\sigma_N$, and the perturbed samples can be built step by step as $x_i = x_{i-1}+\sqrt{\sigma_i^2-\sigma_{i-1}^2}\,z$. If we set $\sigma_i=\sigma(i\Delta t)$, then $\sqrt{\sigma^2(t+\Delta t)-\sigma^2(t)}\approx\sqrt{\tfrac{d[\sigma^2]}{dt}\Delta t}$, and the chain becomes the Euler-Maruyama discretization of

$$
dx = \sqrt{\frac{d[\sigma^2(t)]}{dt}}\,dw,\qquad\text{so}\qquad f=0,\quad g=\sqrt{\frac{d[\sigma^2(t)]}{dt}},\quad x_t = x_0+\sigma_tz.
$$ {#eq-ve-sde}

Since $\int_0^tg^2 = \sigma_t^2-\sigma_0^2$, the kernel is $\mathcal{N}(x_0,(\sigma_t^2-\sigma_0^2)I)\approx\mathcal{N}(x_0,\sigma_t^2I)$. Its variance becomes very large, hence the name variance exploding. Differentiating $\log p_{0t}(x_t\mid x_0) = -\Vert x_t-x_0\Vert^2/2\sigma_t^2+\text{const}$, as slide 33 does, gives $\nabla\log p_{0t} = -(x_t-x_0)/\sigma_t^2$. With the weight $\sigma_t^2$, @eq-dsm becomes

$$
\min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}\Big\Vert\sigma_t\,s_\theta(x_t,t)+\frac{x_t-x_0}{\sigma_t}\Big\Vert^2 = \min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}\big\Vert\sigma_t\,s_\theta(x_t,t)+z\big\Vert^2 .
$$ {#eq-ve-loss}

To obtain the sampler, set $f=0$ in @eq-reverse-sde. A step from $t_i$ to $t_{i-1}$ has $g^2|\Delta t|\approx\sigma_i^2-\sigma_{i-1}^2$, which gives the update on slide 32,

$$
x_{i-1} = x_i + (\sigma_i^2-\sigma_{i-1}^2)\,s_\theta(x_i,i) + \sqrt{\sigma_i^2-\sigma_{i-1}^2}\,z.
$$ {#eq-ve-sampler}

Apart from a factor of 2 in the noise variance, this has the form of a Langevin step (@eq-langevin) with step size $\sigma_i^2-\sigma_{i-1}^2$, which is why the slides call it a Langevin sampler.

### DDPM as the VP SDE

With $\beta_i = \beta(t_i)\Delta t$ and $\sqrt{1-u} = 1-\frac u2+O(u^2)$, the chain $x_i = \sqrt{1-\beta_i}\,x_{i-1}+\sqrt{\beta_i}\,z_{i-1}$ becomes (slide 34)

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(t+\Delta t) &= \sqrt{1-\beta(t+\Delta t)\Delta t}\,x(t) + \sqrt{\beta(t+\Delta t)\Delta t}\,z(t)\\
&\approx x(t) - \tfrac12\beta(t)\Delta t\,x(t) + \sqrt{\beta(t)\Delta t}\,z(t),
\end{aligned}
$$

with errors of order $\Delta t^2$ in the drift and $\Delta t^{3/2}$ in the noise. This is the Euler-Maruyama discretization of

$$
dx = -\tfrac12\beta(t)\,x\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dw.
$$ {#eq-vp-sde}

Because the SDE is linear, $x_t$ given $x_0$ is Gaussian. Its mean solves $\dot{m} = -\frac12\beta m$. For a single centred coordinate $y$, Ito's formula gives $d(y^2) = (-\beta y^2+\beta)dt + 2\sqrt\beta\,y\,dw$, so the variance solves $\dot v = -\beta(v-1)$ with $v(0)=0$. Together these give

$$
p_{0t}(x_t\mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\,x_0,(1-\bar\alpha(t))I\big),\qquad \bar\alpha(t) = e^{-\int_0^t\beta(s)ds},
$$ {#eq-vp-kernel}

which is the continuous limit of $\bar\alpha_i = \prod(1-\beta_j)$. If the data have unit covariance, then so does $x_t$ for every $t$, hence the name variance preserving.

For the loss (slide 35), $\nabla\log p_{0t} = -(x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0)/(1-\bar\alpha_t) = -\epsilon/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$. With the weight $1-\bar\alpha_t$, @eq-dsm becomes

$$
\min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}\big\Vert\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,s_\theta(x_t,t)+\epsilon\big\Vert^2 = \min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}\big\Vert\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)-\epsilon\big\Vert^2,\qquad
\epsilon_\theta = -\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,s_\theta .
$$ {#eq-vp-loss}

The DDPM loss is denoising score matching for the VP SDE, in agreement with @eq-epsilon-score-conversion. The samplers also agree. The reverse Euler-Maruyama step $x_{i-1} = x_i+\frac12\beta_ix_i+\beta_is_\theta+\sqrt{\beta_i}z$ coincides with the DDPM ancestral step $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta_i}}(x_i+\beta_is_\theta)+\sqrt{\beta_i}z$ up to terms of order $\beta_i^2$.

### One SDE, many models

Slide 36 summarizes the general recipe. Choosing an SDE determines the transition kernel, the kernel determines the DSM loss, and the learned score determines the reverse sampler. @tbl-ve-vp shows the recipe for SMLD and DDPM. Both are special cases, as is DDIM through @eq-pf-sigma, and training a diffusion model amounts to training a score function.

| | VE SDE (SMLD) | VP SDE (DDPM) |
|---|---|---|
| $f(x,t)$ and $g(t)$ | $0$ and $\sqrt{d[\sigma^2]/dt}$ | $-\frac12\beta(t)x$ and $\sqrt{\beta(t)}$ |
| kernel $p_{0t}$ | $\mathcal{N}(x_0,\sigma_t^2I)$ | $\mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_t)I)$ |
| DSM target and weight | $-z/\sigma_t$ and $\sigma_t^2$ | $-\epsilon/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$ and $1-\bar\alpha_t$ |
| prior $p_T$ | $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\max}^2I)$ | $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ |

: SMLD and DDPM as two instances of @eq-forward-sde. {#tbl-ve-vp}

### Time embedding

One network has to serve a thousand noise levels, or a continuum of them, which
is what slide 38 means by calling the time embedding the key. The network
$\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ is a U-Net and $t$ reaches it along a separate path,
in three steps.

First the scalar $t$ is lifted to a vector by sinusoidal features
[@ho2020], or by random Gaussian Fourier features in continuous time [@sde],

$$
e(t) = \big[\sin(\omega_1t),\cos(\omega_1t),\dots,
            \sin(\omega_{d/2}t),\cos(\omega_{d/2}t)\big]^\top ,
$$ {#eq-time-features}

a scalar being too weak an input to condition a large network on. Then $e(t)$
passes through two or more fully connected layers with a smooth nonlinearity,
giving a learned embedding $h(t)$. Finally $h(t)$ is injected into *every*
resolution block of the encoder, the bottleneck and the decoder, either added
to the block's features after a projection or used to scale and shift a
normalization layer,
$\mathrm{AdaGN}(u,t) = \kappa(t)\,\mathrm{GroupNorm}(u)+\xi(t)$ [@dhariwal2021].

Injecting $t$ at every scale rather than once at the input is what the
architecture needs, as @fig-unet-time shows: the coarse layers carry global structure, which is what
survives at large $t$, and the outer layers carry edges and texture, which only
matter at small $t$. A single network conditioned on $t$ can move between those
regimes; $N$ separate networks would each see $1/N$ of the data and share
nothing.

![The time-conditioned U-Net of slide 38. The noisy image $x_t$ passes through a multi-scale encoder-decoder that predicts $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$, while the scalar $t$ is encoded by @eq-time-features, transformed by fully connected layers, and injected into every resolution block.](figures/lec07/deb-kit2-fig3-unet-time-embedding.png){#fig-unet-time width=95%}

The network is trained only on inputs whose actual noise level matches $t$, so if a sampler produces an $x_t$ with the wrong noise level, the network receives an input it has never seen and errors appear. The next chapter gives a geometric picture of this effect, where it follows a sample from one noisy manifold to the next.

## A worked example in one dimension {#sec-worked}

Take $p_0 = 0.2\,\mathcal{N}(-2,0.25^2)+0.8\,\mathcal{N}(2,0.25^2)$ and the VP SDE with $\beta(t) = 0.1+19.9t$ on $[0,1]$ as in @sde, so that $\bar\alpha(t) = e^{-0.1t-9.95t^2}$. If we write $p_0 = \sum_j\pi_j\mathcal{N}(m_j,\rho_j^2)$, then @eq-vp-kernel shows that $p_t$ is again a Gaussian mixture, with means $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}m_j$ and variances $v_j = \bar\alpha_t\rho_j^2+1-\bar\alpha_t$. Let $r_j(x)$ be the responsibility of component $j$, which is proportional to $\pi_j$ times the density of $\mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}m_j,v_j)$ at $x$. The exact score is then $\sum_jr_j(x)(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}m_j-x)/v_j$, and @eq-epsilon-score-conversion gives the optimal noise predictor. The script below uses NumPy and SciPy and runs in about 20 seconds. It performs all the numerical checks quoted in this note.

```{.python}
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import wasserstein_distance

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
randn = lambda shape: rng.standard_normal(shape)
W, MU, S = np.array([0.2, 0.8]), np.array([-2.0, 2.0]), np.array([0.25, 0.25])
B0, B1 = 0.1, 20.0
beta = lambda t: B0 + t * (B1 - B0)
abar = lambda t: np.exp(-(B0 * t + 0.5 * (B1 - B0) * t**2))

def score(x, t):
    a = abar(t); m = np.sqrt(a) * MU; v = a * S**2 + 1 - a
    x = np.asarray(x, float)[..., None]
    logn = np.log(W) - 0.5 * (x - m)**2 / v - 0.5 * np.log(v)
    r = np.exp(logn - np.logaddexp.reduce(logn, axis=-1)[..., None])
    return np.sum(r * (m - x) / v, axis=-1)
eps_star = lambda x, t: -np.sqrt(1 - abar(t)) * score(x, t)
def sample_p0(n):
    k = rng.choice(2, size=n, p=W); return MU[k] + S[k] * randn(n)

def reverse_sde(x, n):
    ts = np.linspace(1, 0, n + 1); dt = 1 / n
    for t in ts[:-1]:
        b = beta(t)
        drift = 0.5 * b * x + b * score(x, t)
        x = x + drift * dt + np.sqrt(b * dt) * randn(x.shape)
    return x

def ddim(x, n, eta=0.0, eta_max=False):
    ts = np.linspace(1, 0, n + 1)
    for t, s in zip(ts[:-1], ts[1:]):
        at, as_ = abar(t), abar(s); e = eps_star(x, t)
        x0 = (x - np.sqrt(1 - at) * e) / np.sqrt(at)
        bt2 = (1 - as_) / (1 - at) * (1 - at / as_)
        g2 = (1 - as_) if eta_max else eta**2 * bt2
        x = (np.sqrt(as_) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - as_ - g2) * e
             + np.sqrt(g2) * randn(x.shape))
    return x

def langevin(x, t, n=2000, step=0.01):
    for _ in range(n):
        x = x + step * score(x, t) + np.sqrt(2 * step) * randn(x.shape)
    return x

t, n = 0.3, 1_000_000
x0, eps = sample_p0(n), randn(n)
xt = np.sqrt(abar(t)) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - abar(t)) * eps
for a, b in [(-1.0, 0.0), (-0.5, 0.3), (0.2, -1.0)]:
    s = a * xt + b
    esm = np.mean((s - score(xt, t))**2)
    dsm = np.mean((s + eps / np.sqrt(1 - abar(t)))**2)
    print(f"theta=({a:+.1f},{b:+.1f})  ESM={esm:.4f}  DSM={dsm:.4f}  "
          f"DSM-ESM={dsm - esm:.4f}")

ref, xT = sample_p0(400_000), randn(20_000)
def report(name, x):
    w1 = wasserstein_distance(x, ref)
    print(f"{name:30s} mass(x>0)={np.mean(x > 0):.3f}  W1={w1:.3f}  "
          f"sd={np.std(x):.2f}")
report("Langevin, clean score only", langevin(randn(20_000), t=0.0))
report("reverse SDE, 1000 steps", reverse_sde(xT, 1000))
for n in (10, 50, 500):
    report(f"DDIM eta=0, {n} steps", ddim(xT, n, eta=0.0))
    report(f"DDIM eta=1 (DDPM), {n} steps", ddim(xT, n, eta=1.0))
    report(f"eta=eta_max, {n} steps", ddim(xT, n, eta_max=True))

ts = np.linspace(1, 0, 1001); worst = 0.0
for t, s in zip(ts[:-1], ts[1:]):
    at, as_ = abar(t), abar(s); al = at / as_
    bt2 = (1 - as_) / (1 - at) * (1 - al)
    ddim_e = -np.sqrt(as_ * (1 - at) / at) + np.sqrt(1 - as_ - bt2)
    ddpm_e = -(1 - al) / np.sqrt(al * (1 - at))
    worst = max(worst, abs(np.sqrt(as_ / at) - 1 / np.sqrt(al)),
                abs(ddim_e - ddpm_e))
print(f"largest coefficient difference, eta=1 vs DDPM = {worst:.1e}")

def ddim_invert(x, n):
    ts = np.linspace(0, 1, n + 1)
    for t, u in zip(ts[:-1], ts[1:]):
        t = max(t, 1e-6); at, au = abar(t), abar(u); e = eps_star(x, t)
        x = (np.sqrt(au) * (x - np.sqrt(1 - at) * e) / np.sqrt(at)
             + np.sqrt(1 - au) * e)
    return x
x0 = sample_p0(5000)
for n in (10, 50, 500):
    err = np.mean(np.abs(ddim(ddim_invert(x0, n), n) - x0))
    print(f"inversion, {n} steps, mean |error| = {err:.3f}")

for d in (10, 100, 1000, 10000):
    r = np.linalg.norm(randn((2000, d)), axis=1) / np.sqrt(d)
    print(f"n={d:5d}  |X|/sqrt(n) mean={r.mean():.3f} sd={r.std():.4f}")
d, k = 1000, 100
x = np.zeros((2000, d)); x[:, :k] = 5 * randn((2000, k))
y = x + randn((2000, d))
dist = np.linalg.norm(y[:, k:], axis=1)
print(f"dist(y, V) / sqrt(n-k) mean={np.mean(dist) / np.sqrt(d - k):.3f}")

for _ in range(3):
    w1 = wasserstein_distance(sample_p0(20_000), ref)
    print(f"W1 between a fresh sample of p0 and the reference = {w1:.3f}")
```

For the comparison between DSM and ESM we used linear models $s_\theta(x)=ax+b$. The ESM and DSM losses of the three models are (1.301, 1.870), (0.502, 1.072) and (2.274, 2.846), and their differences 0.5695, 0.5699 and 0.5713 agree up to Monte Carlo error, as @thm-dsm predicts. The coefficients of the $\eta=1$ sampler and of DDPM agree to within $9\times10^{-16}$, which confirms the reduction of @eq-ddpm-in-ddim-form. The DDIM round trip $x_0\to x_T\to x_0$ has a mean error of 0.295, 0.069 and 0.007 with 10, 50 and 500 steps, so the inversion that DiffusionCLIP relies on becomes almost exact. For the shell theorem with $n = 10$, 100, 1000 and 10000, the ratio $\Vert X\Vert/\sqrt n$ has means 0.969, 0.999, 1.000 and 1.000, and its standard deviations 0.221, 0.071, 0.023 and 0.007 are in line with $1/\sqrt{2n}$. The distance to a 100-dimensional subspace in $n=1000$ dimensions is $0.999\sqrt{n-k}$.

@tbl-toy compares the samplers by the mass on the larger mode, the 1-Wasserstein distance (W1) to a reference sample of $p_0$, and the standard deviation. The reverse SDE and DDIM start from the same 20,000 draws of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, and Langevin starts from an independent set. For comparison, a fresh sample of $p_0$ of the same size is between 0.005 and 0.015 away from the reference sample in W1, which is the noise floor for this column.

| sampler | steps | mass on $x>0$ (true 0.8) | W1 | std (true 1.62) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Langevin, clean score only | 2000 | 0.509 | 1.155 | 2.01 |
| reverse SDE | 1000 | 0.799 | 0.005 | 1.62 |
| DDIM, $\eta=0$ | 10 / 50 / 500 | 0.813 / 0.798 / 0.795 | 0.128 / 0.020 / 0.021 | 1.52 / 1.61 / 1.63 |
| DDIM, $\eta=1$ (DDPM) | 10 / 50 / 500 | 0.844 / 0.805 / 0.805 | 0.252 / 0.054 / 0.028 | 1.42 / 1.59 / 1.60 |
| $\eta=\eta_{\max}$ (renoise only) | 10 / 50 / 500 | 0.891 / 0.890 / 0.884 | 0.441 / 0.413 / 0.381 | 1.23 / 1.26 / 1.29 |

: Samplers on the two-mode example with the exact score. {#tbl-toy}

Langevin with the clean score alone does not mix between the modes within 2000 steps, so its mode weights are wrong. With few steps the deterministic sampler is the most accurate (a W1 of 0.128 against 0.252 at 10 steps), a reason DDIM is popular for fast sampling. The renoise-only step with the posterior-mean denoiser remains biased even with many steps.

## Connections and further reading

In the score-based view, conditioning (the topic of lecture 08) amounts to adding a term to the score in @eq-reverse-sde. The manifold picture also underlies many diffusion-based solvers for inverse problems [@chung2022mcg; @chung2024dds].
